sub: How unopposed estrogen builds endometrial hyperplasia and type I cancer, how fibroids and adenomyosis differ, and where endometriosis hides.

pretest.q: Which finding in endometrial hyperplasia best predicts progression to carcinoma?
pretest.why: Atypia, meaning enlarged rounded nuclei with prominent nucleoli, separates atypical hyperplasia (EIN) from hyperplasia without atypia and marks a lesion that often coexists with or becomes endometrioid carcinoma.

w.Cystic gland dilation: Cystic dilation reflects retained secretions in proliferative glands and is common in benign hyperplasia without atypia, which progresses to cancer in only about one to three percent of cases.
w.Crowded glands: Crowding defines hyperplasia in the first place and is present in both low-risk and high-risk forms, so it cannot tell which lesions will turn malignant; the nuclei decide that.
w.Stromal mitoses: Mitoses in the stroma occur normally during the proliferative phase under estrogen and in benign hyperplasia; they signal estrogen drive rather than neoplastic transformation of glandular cells.

pretest.q: Which molecular alteration is an early, central event in serous endometrial carcinoma?
pretest.why: Serous carcinoma arises from a TP53-mutated intraepithelial precursor in atrophic endometrium, producing aberrant p53 staining and aggressive behavior; PTEN and mismatch repair changes belong to estrogen-driven endometrioid carcinoma.

w.PTEN loss: PTEN loss is an early event in estrogen-driven endometrioid carcinoma and atypical hyperplasia, which arise in obese, perimenopausal women rather than in the atrophic endometrium of older women with serous tumors.
w.Mismatch repair defect: Defective mismatch repair, sporadic or inherited in Lynch syndrome, creates microsatellite instability in endometrioid tumors; serous carcinoma instead shows chromosomal instability caused by TP53 loss.
w.MED12 mutation: MED12 mutations occur in up to seventy percent of leiomyomas, benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium, and are not a driver of serous carcinoma of the endometrium.

pretest.q: Which lesion consists of endometrial glands and stroma lying within the myometrium?
pretest.why: Adenomyosis is basalis-type tissue embedded in the uterine wall, where it provokes muscle thickening and a globular, tender uterus; endometriosis lies outside the uterus and a leiomyoma is a pure smooth muscle tumor.

w.Leiomyoma: A leiomyoma is a benign whorled smooth muscle tumor with no glandular component; it produces an asymmetric, nodular uterus rather than diffuse globular enlargement, and it shrinks after menopause.
w.Endometriosis: Endometriosis places glands and stroma outside the uterus, on ovaries and peritoneum, so the uterus stays normal in size and the muscular wall itself is not involved.
w.Endometrial polyp: A polyp is a localized overgrowth of glands and stroma projecting into the cavity from the surface, causing irregular bleeding; it does not extend into the muscle layer.

body: Why does estrogen without progesterone threaten the endometrium?

The uterine wall has two working layers: the myometrium, smooth muscle that contracts, and the **endometrium**, a lining whose surface layer, the functionalis, is rebuilt every cycle from the deeper **basalis**. In the proliferative phase, estrogen makes glands lengthen and divide. After ovulation the corpus luteum adds progesterone, which stops growth, turns glands secretory and, when it falls, ends in shedding. If ovulation fails, progesterone never arrives and estrogen keeps driving mitoses. This **unopposed estrogen** causes endometrial hyperplasia and most endometrial cancer.

Unopposed estrogen has three sources: more estrogen, more years of exposure, or too little progesterone. **Obesity** is the commonest, because adipose aromatase converts androgens to estrogen. Anovulation, as in polycystic ovary syndrome or the perimenopause, removes progesterone, while granulosa cell tumors and estrogen-only therapy add estrogen. Tamoxifen is a partial agonist at the endometrium. Early menarche, late menopause and nulliparity lengthen exposure, and diabetes adds risk. Progestins, **combined oral contraceptives** and pregnancy protect.

**Polycystic ovary syndrome** (PCOS) is the commonest cause of chronic anovulation in young women, so it shows this mechanism clearly; the full syndrome is taught with amenorrhea. Insulin resistance raises insulin levels, and insulin acts with LH on theca cells to increase ovarian androgen output while it lowers sex hormone-binding globulin, so free androgens rise. The resulting **hyperandrogenism** arrests follicles, ovulation fails, no corpus luteum forms and progesterone is absent. The ovaries are enlarged, with a thick, smooth, pearly capsule, many small subcapsular follicular cysts (the "string of pearls" on ultrasound) and thickened stroma with theca cell hyperplasia, but no corpora lutea. Androgens are also aromatized in fat to estrone, so the endometrium sees constant, unopposed estrogen, and these women have a higher risk of hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma, even in their twenties and thirties. A progestin, taken cyclically or as an IUD, protects the lining.
Unopposed estrogen is the common thread

Anything that raises estrogen or lowers progesterone raises the risk of hyperplasia and **type I endometrial carcinoma**: obesity, anovulation, nulliparity, estrogen-only therapy and tamoxifen. Progestins, combined oral contraceptives and pregnancy protect, which is also why a progestin is used to treat hyperplasia without atypia.
Why does estrogen without progesterone lead from hyperplasia to cancer?

Estrogen switches on genes for cell division, so the lining keeps adding mitoses. Progesterone is the brake: it stops division, matures glands into the secretory state, lowers estrogen receptor levels, inactivates estradiol and, when it falls, triggers shedding that resets the count of dividing cells. Without ovulation the brake never engages, glands crowd, and every extra division is another chance for a mutation. Early hits such as PTEN loss let crowded glands escape growth control, and atypia appears as mutations accumulate.
How does hyperplasia progress to endometrioid carcinoma?

Endometrial hyperplasia is a gland overgrowth with a higher gland-to-stroma ratio than normal proliferative endometrium. **Hyperplasia without atypia** has crowded, sometimes cystic glands with normal nuclei and carries about a 1 to 3 percent cancer risk, so a progestin can reverse it. **Hyperplasia with atypia**, also called {{rp14_ein|endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia}}, has complex glands with enlarged, rounded nuclei and prominent nucleoli, often with PTEN loss, and it frequently coexists with carcinoma. Both cause abnormal bleeding, and cytologic **atypia** is the best predictor of cancer. Atypia is treated by hysterectomy, or by high-dose progestin with close biopsy follow-up when fertility is wanted.
Crowded glands alone do not predict cancer

A thick lining or crowded, cystic glands suggests hyperplasia, but without atypia the cancer risk stays low and a progestin is enough. Hyperplasia with **atypia** is the lesion that predicts cancer and prompts hysterectomy, and because a small biopsy can undersample, it calls for a search for coexisting carcinoma.
How do type I and type II endometrial carcinoma differ?

**Endometrial carcinoma** is the most common gynecologic cancer in the United States, although ovarian cancer kills more women. It peaks at 55 to 65 years, and postmenopausal bleeding is the presenting sign, so many are found early. About 80 percent are **type I** endometrioid carcinomas: low-grade glands resembling proliferative endometrium, arising from atypical hyperplasia in estrogen-rich women, with early PTEN loss and mismatch repair defects. They are indolent and stay localized for years. Most of the rest are **type II**, serous or clear cell carcinomas of older, thin women with atrophic endometrium. Serous carcinoma starts with an early TP53 mutation, forms papillae with psammoma bodies, shows diffuse p53 staining and spreads early through the peritoneum, so it is aggressive.
Type II serous or clear cell
Indolent: low grade, localized, good prognosis
Aggressive: high grade, early spread, poor prognosis

Endometrial cancer is staged surgically, and the stage follows how far the tumor has grown. {{rp14_myoinv|Myometrial invasion}} of less than half the wall thickness is stage IA and carries an excellent outlook; invasion of half or more (IB) raises the chance of nodal spread. Extension into the cervical stroma is stage II, spread to the serosa, adnexa or lymph nodes is stage III, and bladder, bowel or distant disease is stage IV; nodal spread goes to the pelvic and para-aortic nodes. Most type I tumors are found at stage I, where five-year survival exceeds 90 percent, whereas serous carcinoma often presents at an advanced stage.

Postmenopausal bleeding is any bleeding after 12 months without a period, and about 1 in 10 patients has endometrial cancer. Atrophy of the endometrium or vagina is the commonest cause, followed by polyps and by exogenous estrogen, which includes hormone therapy and, at the endometrium, tamoxifen. Hyperplasia and carcinoma are less common but must not be missed, so the work-up is built around finding them.
Evaluating postmenopausal bleeding step by step
Examine the vulva, vagina and cervix first. Atrophy, the most common cause, a cervical lesion or a polyp can be mistaken for uterine bleeding.
Measure the lining or sample it

Transvaginal ultrasonography measures endometrial thickness; a lining of 4 mm or less makes cancer very unlikely, while a thicker one needs tissue. Many clinicians go straight to an office **endometrial biopsy**, a thin suction catheter that samples the lining without anesthesia.
Escalate when the blind sample fails

If the biopsy is inadequate, or bleeding persists after a benign result, **hysteroscopy** shows the cavity and takes directed biopsies, and **dilation and curettage** (D&C) scrapes the lining under anesthesia.
Treat by diagnosis, and stage cancer surgically

Atrophy needs topical estrogen, and polyps are removed hysteroscopically. Hyperplasia gets progestin or hysterectomy. Carcinoma needs surgical **staging**: hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and lymph node assessment.
A blind suction sample of the lining, taken in the office
First tissue test; a positive result is reliable, but a negative one with ongoing bleeding needs more
A direct view of the cavity with targeted samples
A focal lesion, a polyp or submucosal fibroid, or an inadequate office sample
A scraping of the whole lining under anesthesia
An unobtainable or inadequate office sample, as with cervical stenosis, or removal of retained tissue
Where do Lynch syndrome, Cowden syndrome and carcinosarcoma fit?

**Lynch syndrome** is an autosomal dominant germline defect in a DNA {{rp14_mmr|mismatch repair}} gene, most often MLH1 or MSH2. Unrepaired replication errors cause microsatellite instability, and the tumors lose nuclear staining for the missing protein. Carriers develop colorectal cancer, and the endometrium is the next most common site, followed by ovary, stomach and urinary tract. **Cowden syndrome** is a different inherited route: a germline PTEN mutation causes hamartomas and raises the risk of breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer. Endometrial carcinoma in a young woman, or lost mismatch repair staining, prompts genetic counseling.

**Carcinosarcoma**, also called malignant mixed Müllerian tumor, is a **biphasic** tumor: a malignant epithelial part, usually high-grade serous or endometrioid carcinoma, plus a malignant mesenchymal part. The sarcomatous part is homologous when it resembles tissue native to the uterus, such as smooth muscle or stroma, and **heterologous** when it contains foreign tissue such as cartilage, bone or skeletal muscle. Because the uterine epithelium and stroma both come from the Müllerian ducts, one tumor can mix them. Most carcinosarcomas are monoclonal: the sarcomatous part is metaplastic change within a single carcinoma, so they spread like carcinomas. They occur after menopause, usually carry TP53 mutations and behave like high-grade serous carcinoma, and tamoxifen raises the risk.
Endometrial cancer can be the first Lynch cancer

Do not wait for a colon cancer before thinking of Lynch syndrome: the endometrial cancer often comes first, usually an **endometrioid** tumor with lost mismatch repair staining. An elderly, thin woman with a papillary, p53-mutated serous tumor has sporadic type II disease instead.
How do leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma and adenomyosis differ?

A **leiomyoma**, or fibroid, is the most common tumor in women: a benign, sharply circumscribed, gray-white smooth muscle nodule with a firm, {{rp14_whorl|whorled}} cut surface. Estrogen and progesterone drive its growth, so fibroids enlarge in pregnancy and shrink after menopause, and they are two to three times more common in Black women. Submucosal fibroids bulge into the cavity and cause heavy bleeding and miscarriage, intramural ones enlarge the uterus, and subserosal ones cause pressure or hang on a stalk. A fibroid can outgrow its blood supply in pregnancy, causing painful red degeneration, and it essentially never becomes a sarcoma.

**Leiomyosarcoma** is a rare malignant smooth muscle tumor that arises de novo, not from a fibroid. It is usually solitary and postmenopausal, a soft, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass. Diagnosis needs cytologic atypia, tumor cell necrosis and a high mitotic rate assessed together, because mitoses alone occur in benign tumors of young women; it recurs often and spreads hematogenously, usually to the lungs. {{rp14_adenomyosis|Adenomyosis}} is not a tumor: endometrial glands and stroma lie within the myometrium, and the muscle thickens around them into a uniformly enlarged, soft, globular uterus with heavy, painful periods, typically in multiparous women in their 40s.
Glands and stroma between muscle bundles
What is endometriosis, and how is it treated?

**Endometriosis** is endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus. The ovary is the usual site, where old blood forms an {{rp14_endometrioma|endometrioma}}, or chocolate cyst, and implants stud the peritoneum, pouch of Douglas and uterosacral ligaments as red-brown, powder-burn nodules. Most cases follow **retrograde menstruation** through the tubes; coelomic metaplasia and lymphatic or vascular spread explain unusual sites. Implants bleed with each cycle, make prostaglandin E2 and express aromatase, so local estrogen feeds an inflammatory loop. Bleeding and scarring make fibrous pelvic adhesions that distort the tubes and ovaries and can obliterate the pouch of Douglas, so patients have dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, painful defecation and infertility, with a normal-sized uterus.

Laparoscopy with biopsy confirms the diagnosis by showing both glands and stroma, often with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Treatment suppresses estrogen-driven growth: NSAIDs for pain, then continuous combined oral contraceptives or progestins, and for persistent pain a **GnRH** agonist such as leuprolide, which desensitizes the pituitary and lowers FSH, LH and estradiol, or the oral antagonist elagolix. **Danazol**, a synthetic androgen, also suppresses gonadotropins but causes acne, hirsutism, voice deepening, weight gain, low HDL cholesterol and liver injury, and it also treats hereditary angioedema. Surgery excises implants, and hysterectomy is a last resort.
Uterine size separates endometriosis from adenomyosis

In endometriosis the tissue lies outside the uterus, so the uterus is normal in size, with cyclic pelvic pain and infertility. In adenomyosis the tissue lies inside the wall, so the whole uterus is soft and globular, with heavy, painful periods. Both are estrogen-dependent and often coexist.
Which benign endometrial problems appear on exams?

An **endometrial polyp** is a focal overgrowth of glands and stroma on a fibrous core that causes irregular bleeding; it is more common with obesity and tamoxifen, and hysteroscopy removes it. Acute endometritis follows delivery, cesarean section or abortion, especially with retained products; it is polymicrobial and shows neutrophils, with fever and a tender uterus. Infection ascends from the cervix and vagina, and the same route carries chlamydia and gonorrhea into the upper genital tract, where a pus-filled tube (pyosalpinx) or a scarred, fluid-filled tube (hydrosalpinx) can result. Chronic endometritis is defined by **plasma cells** in the stroma and follows pelvic inflammatory disease, an IUD, retained tissue or tuberculosis. {{rp14_asherman|Asherman syndrome}} is scarring of the basalis with intrauterine adhesions after curettage or infection, causing secondary amenorrhea and infertility with normal hormone levels.

body.q: A 56-year-old woman taking tamoxifen for breast cancer has vaginal spotting and a thick endometrial stripe. Which reasoning best explains the endometrial response?
o: Tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors everywhere, so the lining thins and bleeds from atrophy
Tamoxifen inhibits aromatase, so rising androgens overgrow the lining
Tamoxifen raises progesterone, so the lining turns secretory and sheds irregularly
Tamoxifen is a partial estrogen agonist in the endometrium, so the lining proliferates while the breast is blocked
body.why: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator whose effect depends on the co-regulators each tissue expresses. In breast cancer cells it blocks estrogen-driven growth, but in the endometrium it acts as a partial agonist, so the lining proliferates without progesterone opposition. That explains polyps, hyperplasia and a modest rise in endometrial cancer, so new bleeding on tamoxifen needs endometrial sampling. Aromatase inhibitors lower estrogen everywhere and do not thicken the lining.
